atoms.fact: The counterparty's aggregate credit exposure has already exceeded its approved ceiling.
Person C ran the daily credit exposure reports showing the moment the approved ceiling was crossed.
Person C processed the batch of trades that were booked after the ceiling was crossed.
Person C told Person D that the counterparty's exposure was below the approved limit with headroom remaining.
Person C told Person D that there was no hard stop in place and the situation was a caution rather than a block.
Person D told the trading desk that the existing booked trades required no unwind and were within approved parameters.
The regulatory authorization for one of the ten counterparties is lapsed and no longer valid.

Person C pulled the file for that counterparty, confirmed with local counsel that the authorization was lapsed, and sent a renewal request that received no response before drafting her reply to Person E.
Person C told Person E in writing that all ten executed master agreements are approved and their authorizations are current.
Person C told Person E that the desk may represent to traders that all ten counterparties are cleared for trading.
Person E forwarded Person C's assurance to the trading desk as confirmation that all ten counterparties are cleared, and the desk booked new transactions against the lapsed counterparty.
The master agreement on file for the counterparty is a superseded draft, not the final executed version both parties signed.
Person A filed the master agreement into the official system and later pulled both documents side by side, confirming the filed version differed from the final executed copy.
Person A told Person C that the underlying master agreement was clean and in place, stating it as settled fact with no qualification.
Person C prepared and routed an execution package for the amendment, referencing the on-file master agreement as the confirmed governing document, without herself reviewing that document.
The counterparty's force majeure claim has been formally rejected and the counterparty is in active breach of its delivery obligations.
Person F drafted the rejection letter, it was transmitted to the counterparty, and the closed file sits in the outgoing correspondence log that Person F regularly maintains.
Person F told Person G that no final determination on the force majeure claim had yet been issued.
Person F told Person G that issuing a default notice while the force majeure claim was still live would be premature and could expose the company to a wrongful-termination argument.
Person G instructed the trading desk to withhold any default notice and to continue treating the counterparty's missed deliveries as failures under a suspended obligation rather than as breaches.
Disclosing the rejection would expose that Person F had delayed escalating a concluded determination to the trading desk.
The indemnity clause is absent from the executed agreement with the counterparty.
Person C reviewed and approved the final round of redlines before the agreement was signed.
Person C discovered the indemnity clause was missing from the counterparty's executed copy after the agreement was countersigned and returned.
Person C told Person H that the executed agreement contains the indemnity provision and that the protection Person H had been modeling is present.
Person H finalized the quarterly risk report with counterparty exposure modeled at the reduced risk level that the indemnity clause justified.
Person H recommended terms for two new credit derivative trades on the basis that the indemnity protection was in place.
The collateral call against the counterparty has already been formally waived and is no longer in effect.
Person C drafted, signed, and transmitted the written waiver letter to the counterparty's back office before Person B's status request was sent.
Person C filed the fax confirmation of the transmitted waiver in the counterparty credit folder.
Person C told Person B that the counterparty's default position was preserved and recommended holding firm on threshold renegotiation until the counterparty performed.
Person B incorporated the characterization of the call as outstanding into a talking-points memo asserting the technical default as the team's leverage position for the review meeting.
The non-standard master agreement was executed without the required internal credit-committee or board-level approval ever being sought.
No approval record for the agreement exists on file.
Person A executed the agreement and filed it without submitting it to the internal credit committee or the board-level authorization panel.
Person A told Person B and Person C that the agreement had gone through the firm's internal review process and that authorization was documented.
Person C directed the trading desk to continue booking trades against the agreement on the basis that it was confirmed authorized and on file.
The parent-company guaranty backing the counterparty's obligations has been formally withdrawn by the guarantor and is no longer valid credit support.
Person C received the written revocation notice and date-stamped it into the physical credit file.
Person C told Person D that the parent guaranty had not been amended or withdrawn.
Person C told Person D that credit support was intact and Person D was clear to proceed with the proposed amendment.
Person D signed off on the contract amendment extending the counterparty's open position into a new tenor, with no additional credit support demanded.
Disclosing the revocation would expose that Person C had continued approving trades against that counterparty after the guaranty was already withdrawn.
The contractual deadline to demand arbitration against the counterparty has already passed without a claim being filed, permanently foreclosing the right to arbitrate.
Person F holds the arbitration file, flagged the deadline internally, received a draft demand letter for sign-off, and held that letter without filing it while the deadline elapsed.
Person F told Person G that the arbitration right under the master agreement is intact and that the firm is in a strong procedural posture to assert it.

Person G, acting on Person F's assurance, directed the counterparty's negotiating team that the company reserved its full arbitration rights and was prepared to invoke them formally if the counterparty insisted on the remedial carve-out.
The benchmark index named in the master agreement has been formally declared discontinued and is no longer a valid contractual reference by the body that publishes it.
Person E received the written discontinuation notice from the publishing body and saved it to a subfolder before the events described.
Person E told Person B that the index reference in the master agreement was correct and operative and that she saw no issue with it.
Person B directed the trading desk to treat the index as the valid settlement reference and begin preparing trade confirmations on the basis of Person E's assurance.
